<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:race}
  Let $T_{1}, \dots, T_{n}$ be independent with $T_{j} \sim \operatorname{Exp}(s_{j})$, and
  let $\sigma$ order the players by increasing clock, so that $\sigma_1$ has the smallest clock.
  Then $\sigma$ has the ICM{} distribution given by \cref{eq:icm}.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The minimum of independent exponentials is attained by player $i$ with probability
  $s_{i} / S$. Conditional on player $i$ having the minimum at time $t$, the residual
  times $T_{j} - t$, $j \neq i$, are again independent exponentials with rates $s_{j}$
  by the memoryless property. Induction over the remaining players gives \cref{eq:icm}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:representation}
  For every player $i$ and every place $r+1$ with $0 \le r \le n-1$,
  \begin{equation}
    Q_{i,r+1} \;=\; \int_{0}^{\infty} s_{i}\, e^{-s_{i} t}\; C^{\setminus i}_{r}(t)\; \mathrm{d}t .
    \label{eq:representation}
  \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:race}, $i$ finishes in place $r+1$ exactly when $r$ clocks are smaller than
  $T_{i}$. Conditional on $T_{i} = t$, the number of smaller clocks is Poisson-binomial
  with the generating function in \cref{eq:loo-pgf}, so the probability that it equals $r$ is
  $C^{\setminus i}_{r}(t)$. Integrating against the density $s_{i} e^{-s_{i} t}$ of $T_{i}$
  gives \cref{eq:representation}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:equity}
  $V_{i} = \int_{0}^{\infty} s_{i} e^{-s_{i} t} \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} \pi_{r+1}
  C^{\setminus i}_{r}(t)\, \mathrm{d}t$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop:truncation}
  Let $t_{\mathrm{L}} = \varphi(x_{\mathrm{L}})$ and $t_{\mathrm{R}} = \varphi(x_{\mathrm{R}})$. Omitting $[0,
  t_{\mathrm{L}})$ from \cref{eq:representation} changes $Q_{i,1}$ by at most $\tilde{s}_{i}
  t_{\mathrm{L}}$, which is a relative error of at most $\widetilde{S}\, t_{\mathrm{L}}$, and
  changes every $Q_{i,r}$ with $r \ge 2$ by at most $\tilde{s}_{i} \widetilde{S}\,
  t_{\mathrm{L}}^{2} / 2$. Omitting $[t_{\mathrm{R}}, \infty)$ changes every $Q_{i,r}$ by at
  most $e^{-\tilde{s}_{i} t_{\mathrm{R}}}$, and every equity of player $i$ by a relative error of
  at most $2\, e^{-\tilde{s}_{i} t_{\mathrm{R}}}$ when $e^{-\tilde{s}_{i} t_{\mathrm{R}}} \le 1/2$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:width}
  Let $g(a) = a^{2} / (2 (e^{a} - 1))$ and $g_{\max} = \max_{a > 0} g(a) \approx 0.324$, attained
  at $a = b^{*} \approx 1.594$. For every $t > 0$,
  \begin{equation}
    \sigma^{2} \;\ge\; \frac{1}{2 \sum_{j \ne i} g(a_j)} \;\ge\; \frac{1}{2 (n - 1)\, g_{\max}} ,
    \label{eq:width}
  \end{equation}
  with equality in the first inequality if and only if all $a_j$ are equal, and in the second if
  and only if moreover $a_j = b^{*}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label[remark]{rem:rounding}
  The coefficients at each node are products and sums of non-negative numbers, and
  \cref{sec:allplayers} delivers them with an absolute error of $O(n u)$; the quadrature
  sum over $M$ positive weights adds $O(M u)$. The resulting floor is
  $O((n + M)u)$ in the worst case and $O(\sqrt{n + M}\, u)$ typically, about
  $10^{-14}$ for $n \approx M \approx 10^{3}$. This accounting is heuristic, and we treat
  the floor as an estimate to be confirmed by measurement (\cref{sec:accuracy}).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:stability}
  Let the computed full-product coefficients satisfy $\sum_r |\widehat{C_{r}} - C_{r}|
  \le \theta$, let $q_{i}$ and $1 - q_{i}$ be evaluated as in
  \cref{sec:fullproduct}, and let \cref{eq:forward} be used when $q_{i} \ge 1/2$ and
  \cref{eq:backward} otherwise, in floating-point arithmetic with unit roundoff $u$. Then
  for every $r$,
  \begin{equation}
    \bigl| \widehat{E^{\setminus i}_{r}} - E^{\setminus i}_{r} \bigr|
    \;\le\; \theta + 7u \sum_{s} C_{s} + O(u^{2})
    \;=\; \theta + 7u + O(u^{2}) .
    \label{eq:stability-bound}
  \end{equation}
  With $\theta$ from \cref{eq:product-error}, every scaled leave-one-out coefficient has absolute
  error at most $(4 + e^{-2})\, n u + 7 u + O(u^{2}) < (4.2\, n + 7)u$,
  uniformly in $r$. If the direction is
  chosen against the rule, the error committed at step $s$ is amplified by
  $\max(\alpha_{i}, 1/\alpha_{i})^{\,|r - s|}$ at step $r$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
A perturbation $\delta$ of the carried value changes the next value by $-\alpha_{i} \delta$ in
  \cref{eq:forward} and by $-\delta / \alpha_{i}$ in \cref{eq:backward}, a factor of modulus at
  most one under the rule, so the error at any step is at most the sum of the local errors of
  the steps traversed. Each local error is a small multiple of $u C_{r}$ plus the error
  of the input coefficient, and the sum over $r$ is bounded because $\sum_r C_{r} = 1$ and
  the input errors sum to $\theta$. \Cref{app:stability} gives the accounting.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:invariant}
  For all $i$ and $r$, $0 \le E^{\setminus i}_{r} \le C_{r}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$C_{r} = E^{\setminus i}_{r} + (1 - q_{i}) C^{\setminus i}_{r-1}$ with both terms non-negative.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:factor}
  For $a \ge 0$ and $|y| < \pi/2$, let $q = \exp(-a e^{iy})$. Then $|q| + |1 - q| \le
  \exp(g_{\max} \tan^{2} y)$, with $g_{\max} = \max_{b > 0} b^{2} / (2 (e^{b} - 1)) \approx 0.324$ as in
  \cref{lem:width}.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Write $\varrho = |q| = e^{-a \cos y} \in (0, 1]$ and $\theta = a \sin y$, so that $q =
  \varrho e^{-i\theta}$ and $|1 - q|^{2} = (1 - \varrho)^{2} + 4\varrho \sin^{2}(\theta / 2)$.
  If $\varrho = 1$ the claim is trivial. Otherwise $\sqrt{A^{2} + B} \le A + B / (2A)$ for $A >
  0$, $B \ge 0$, and $\sin^{2}(\theta / 2) \le \theta^{2} / 4$ give
  \[
    |1 - q| \;\le\; (1 - \varrho) + \frac{\varrho\, a^{2} \sin^{2} y}{2 (1 - \varrho)} ,
  \]
  so that, with $b = a \cos y > 0$ and $\varrho = e^{-b}$,
  \[
    |q| + |1 - q| \;\le\; 1 + \tan^{2} y \cdot \frac{b^{2}}{2 (e^{b} - 1)}
    \;\le\; 1 + g_{\max} \tan^{2} y \;\le\; \exp(g_{\max} \tan^{2} y) . \qedhere
  \]
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:strip}
  For every player $i$, every place $r + 1$, every step $h > 0$ and every $d \in (0,
  \pi/2)$,
  \begin{equation}
    \Bigl| I_h[f] - \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, \mathrm{d}x \Bigr|
    \;\le\; \frac{2 \exp\bigl( (n - 1)\, g_{\max} \tan^{2} d \bigr)}{\cos d \;\bigl( e^{2\pi d / h} - 1 \bigr)} .
    \label{eq:strip}
  \end{equation}
  With $d = \pi / ((n - 1) g_{\max} h) \le 1/2$, that is, for $(n - 1) h \ge 2\pi / g_{\max}
  \approx 19.4$, the right-hand side is at most
  \begin{equation}
    2.3\, \exp\Bigl( -\bigl( 1 - \eta(d) \bigr) \frac{\pi^{2}}{(n - 1)\, g_{\max}\, h^{2}} \Bigr)
    \Bigl( 1 - e^{-2\pi d / h} \Bigr)^{-1},
    \qquad \eta(d) = \frac{\tan^{2} d}{d^{2}} - 1 \le 0.194 .
    \label{eq:rate}
  \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
$f$ is entire. On the line $x = \xi + iy$ we have $e^{x} = e^{\xi} e^{iy}$, so
  $|e^{-\tilde{s}_{i} e^{x}}| = e^{-\tilde{s}_{i} e^{\xi} \cos y}$, $|e^{x}| = e^{\xi}$, and
  $|C^{\setminus i}_{r}(e^{x})| \le \exp((n - 1) g_{\max} \tan^{2} y)$ by the remark above. Substituting
  $\tau = e^{\xi}$,
  \[
    \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(\xi + iy)|\, \mathrm{d}\xi
    \;\le\; \exp\bigl( (n - 1) g_{\max} \tan^{2} y \bigr) \int_{0}^{\infty} \tilde{s}_{i} e^{-\tilde{s}_{i} \tau \cos y}\, \mathrm{d}\tau
    \;=\; \frac{\exp\bigl( (n - 1) g_{\max} \tan^{2} y \bigr)}{\cos y},
  \]
  which is increasing in $|y|$, so $N = \exp((n - 1) g_{\max} \tan^{2} d) / \cos d$ serves for all
  $|y| < d$; the same bounds show that $f \to 0$ uniformly in the strip as $|\xi| \to \infty$.
  The strip theorem gives \cref{eq:strip}. For \cref{eq:rate}, the exponent at $d = \pi / ((n -
  1) g_{\max} h)$ is $(n - 1) g_{\max} d^{2} (1 + \eta(d)) - 2\pi d / h = -(1 - \eta(d))\,
  \pi^{2} / ((n - 1) g_{\max} h^{2})$, and $2 / \cos(1/2) \le 2.3$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
